Persist browser data only when the user value and threat model justify it.

Persistence can make an application feel dependable, but it also gives data a longer life than the current page. This chapter shows how to keep a useful local workspace across refreshes while protecting the value at the persistence boundary and making the security trade-offs explicit.

Why this boundary matters

The FeatureCell continues to work with plain in-memory State while encryption protects the finalized value before persistence writes it to browser storage. Encrypting before persisting keeps storage concerns out of application code, but it is not a complete browser-security strategy: key management, XSS exposure, storage lifetime, and the sensitivity of the data still require deliberate decisions.

Use this structure for

  • restoring non-sensitive preferences across page refreshes
  • keeping a local workspace or draft available during a session
  • retaining browser data when its value justifies its storage lifetime

By the end of this chapter

You will have encryption and Session Storage persistence registered in the correct pipeline boundary, a plain in-memory Feature State, and a clear understanding of what this protection covers—and what your application security design must still address.

Chapter 10 Starting Point, License, and Threat Model

Start with the completed Chapter 9 project. Encryption and persistence are Pro capabilities. This example enables development evaluation with devMode: true and bypassLicensing: true; production use requires a valid license and must not rely on the bypass.

What This Boundary Protects

AES-256-GCM protects the confidentiality and integrity of the persisted envelope when the key-derived secret remains unavailable to an attacker who obtains storage alone. The FeatureCell continues to expose plain State to trusted application code.

What It Does Not Protect
  • Successful same-origin script execution, XSS, malicious extensions, or a compromised browser runtime can read plain in-memory State and any client-available secret.
  • Encryption does not provide authorization, server security, data minimization, retention policy, or cross-device recovery.
  • Never paste production secrets or sensitive user data into this teaching example. Bundled browser JavaScript is not a confidential key store.

Step 34: Configure Encrypt and Persist Behaviors

↑ top

This step adds encryption and persistence to the same character collection. The AES-256 Encrypt behavior protects the finalized pipeline value before the Session Storage Persist behavior writes it to browser storage. The FeatureCell continues to work with plain in-memory State.

Register withAes256EncryptBehavior and withSessionStoragePersistBehavior in app.config.ts. Encrypt and Persist occupy fixed pipeline stages: the finalized plain value is encrypted before the Persist stage writes its envelope. Their position in the behavior declaration array does not redefine that stage order.

Make the Change
  1. Install the package.
  2. Open app.config.ts.
  3. Import withAes256EncryptBehavior and withSessionStoragePersistBehavior from .
  4. Add both behaviors to the behavior list passed to provideFeatureCell(). Declaration order does not override the behaviors' fixed pipeline stages.

Step 35: Encrypt Feature State

↑ top

AES-256-GCM encryption protects the finalized Feature State before it reaches persistence. It runs after Resolve, Merge, Operators, Filters, and Reducers have completed, so the FeatureCell continues to expose the same plain in-memory value to the application.

The example uses a client-visible tutorial secret and a stable salt so you can repeat the exercise and decrypt the same persisted envelope after a reload. The salt is not a password or confidential key; it supports key derivation and must remain stable for ciphertext that must be read later. Production key management is an application-security decision. Do not treat a secret bundled with browser code as confidential.

Make the Change
  1. In example.service.ts, export the stable 16-byte EXAMPLE_AES256_SALT. Before initialize(), call setAes256Secret() with the tutorial secret, that salt, and 250_000 PBKDF2 iterations.
  2. Treat aes256Secret as PBKDF2 input key material, salt as non-secret derivation input, and iterations as derivation cost. The behavior generates and stores the AES-GCM initialization vector in the encrypted envelope; do not substitute the stable salt for that per-encryption IV.
  3. Use the Results panel to compare plain Feature State with the encrypted envelope. Confirm the envelope contains version, iv, data, and alg: 'AES-256-GCM' fields rather than plain character JSON.
What to Look For
  • Encryption does not change the value exposed by the FeatureCell.
  • AES-256-GCM provides confidentiality and integrity at the persistence boundary.
  • A stable salt is required to decrypt previously persisted ciphertext.
  • The salt may be stored with or alongside ciphertext; security depends on protecting the secret/key material and the running application, not on hiding the salt.

Step 36: Persist Feature State

↑ top

Add withSessionStoragePersistBehavior after encryption to store the encrypted envelope in browser sessionStorage. Refresh the page and the persisted state remains available in that same tab. Close the tab and the session normally ends, so it is not durable application storage. Browsers can restore a previous session after a crash or through session-restoration features, so do not treat tab closure as a guaranteed erasure boundary.

The example intentionally provides initialState while allowing persisted State to take priority. During hydration the persisted value is used by design; the initial value is not loaded into the active FeatureCell and is overwritten with undefined when no persisted value is available. This makes the persistence boundary explicit instead of silently mixing two sources of truth.

Persistence Outcomes in This Example
  • Valid persisted envelope: decrypt, hydrate, and use the persisted value instead of initialState.
  • No persisted envelope: this configured persistence path exposes no restored value, so inspect hasValue and the displayed undefined result rather than assuming an initial-value fallback.
  • Malformed storage JSON: the Session Storage behavior returns undefined. A valid JSON AES envelope that cannot be decrypted rejects instead of returning partial plaintext.
Recovery Scope

The interactive example demonstrates valid persistence, same-tab reload, and missing storage. It does not provide a button that injects corrupted ciphertext. The behavior tests—not this UI—establish that malformed JSON loads as undefined and AES decryption failure rejects. For this tutorial, clear only EXAMPLE_ENCRYPTED_STORAGE_KEY, report the normalized failure, and require a fresh authoritative load. Never clear all origin storage, silently accept, or partially parse damaged data.

Make the Change
  1. Persisted state is handled through the pipeline. Once registered in the there is nothing more to configure.
  2. Make a character change and inspect the persisted output.
  3. Open the browser developer tools Application or Storage panel, select Session Storage, and find the namespaced key exported as EXAMPLE_ENCRYPTED_STORAGE_KEY in example.service.ts. Confirm the stored value is an encrypted envelope rather than plain character JSON.
  4. Refresh the page in the same tab and verify that the collection is restored.
What to Look For
  • Persist observes the finalized value after encryption and does not participate in state computation.
  • Session storage is scoped to one tab and survives reloads only within that tab.
  • Persisted State takes priority over initialState by design.

  2. Close the tab, open the example again, and confirm that the tab-scoped value is gone.
